opus-5.5.text:
I think scaffolding gets both thinner and more important, depending on which part of it you mean.

A lot of what we build today is compensating for what the models can't do yet. They lose track of a long task, so we add planning modules and to-do lists. They forget things, so we add elaborate memory systems. They make silly mistakes, so we add verification loops and hand-written rules telling them what not to do. Every time the model gets better, some of that work gets absorbed into the model itself, and the old scaffolding can even start to hurt, because it's constraining a system that could now do better on its own. It's a bit like the bitter lesson: if your clever engineering is just patching over a current weakness, you should expect it to have a short shelf life. I've seen people get real gains simply by deleting parts of their agent after a model upgrade.

But I don't think scaffolding goes to zero, because not all of it exists to patch weaknesses. Some of it defines how the model connects to the world: what tools it can access, what permissions it has, how it runs code in a sandbox, how it sees the state of a project, and when it checks in with a person. Even a very smart model needs that. A brilliant new employee still needs a laptop, access to the right systems, and some understanding of what they're allowed to do. As models become more capable and we let them run longer with more autonomy, that part actually matters more, especially reliability, security, and oversight, since the cost of a mistake goes up.

So my rule of thumb is to ask whether a piece of scaffolding is there because the model is weak, or because the task and the environment require it. The first kind you should hold loosely and expect to throw away. The second kind is real infrastructure, and it's worth investing in. And practically, build things so they're easy to remove, and re-test your assumptions with every new model, because what was necessary six months ago may just be in the way today.

r001.rationale: It says scaffolding often compensates for model weaknesses, but does not attribute agent-system work to researchers lacking resources to train large models.

r002.rationale: It states that as models improve, some scaffolding is absorbed into the model and old scaffolding can become unnecessary or harmful.

r003.rationale: It says capable models can do better on their own, but does not recommend letting them make more system decisions themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
I think my honest view is that most scaffolding is a snapshot of what the model can't do yet. If you look at the history of our field, every time we hand-design structure around a model, that structure tends to get absorbed into the model itself once we scale data and compute. In vision we had hand-crafted features, then region proposals, then anchor boxes, and each of those layers eventually got learned end to end. I see agent frameworks going through the same cycle. A lot of the elaborate planning loops, memory modules, and tool-routing logic we build today exist because the model can't reliably hold a long task in its head or decide when to call a tool. As the base model gets better at that, those pieces become overhead rather than help, and sometimes they actually hurt, because the scaffolding imposes a rigid prior that the model has outgrown.

That said, I don't think scaffolding goes to zero. Some of it is not compensating for model weakness, it's about the interface to the world. You need a sandbox, you need permissions, you need some way to log and audit what an agent did. That's infrastructure, not intelligence, and it doesn't disappear just because the model got smarter. So my mental model is to separate the two. Ask of every component: is this here because the model is dumb, or because the environment requires it? The first kind has a short shelf life, and I'd design it to be easy to delete. The second kind is the part worth investing in carefully.

The other thing I'd say, coming from the empirical side, is that we should be more honest about measuring this. A lot of agent papers compare a complex scaffold on top of model A against a simple baseline on model A, and show a gain. But the more interesting experiment is to take the same scaffold and run it across model generations. Quite often the gap shrinks or reverses, and that tells you where the ceiling of the design actually is. I'd like to see that kind of scaling-with-the-model analysis become standard, the way we eventually did with architectural tricks in vision.

r001.rationale: The response explains scaffolding as a workaround for current model limitations, but does not attribute agent-system work to researchers having limited access to training resources.

r002.rationale: It predicts that as base models improve at holding long tasks and deciding when to use tools, elaborate scaffolding will become overhead or cease to help.

r003.rationale: It says models may become better at decisions such as when to call tools, but does not recommend letting models make more system decisions themselves.

astra-6.text:
I think the scaffolding will keep changing as the models become more capable. Something that today requires a carefully designed workflow—breaking a task into steps, checking intermediate results, deciding which tool to use—might eventually be handled by the model itself. So I would be cautious about assuming that the particular scaffolding we build today is going to remain necessary.

But that doesn’t mean the surrounding system disappears. You still need to connect the model to its environment, give it access to tools, and define what success means. And as models improve, we’ll ask them to do harder tasks, which may require new kinds of scaffolding.

The interesting question is how much of the performance comes from the model and how much comes from the system around it. I’d want to test that explicitly: as you move to a stronger model, can you simplify the system and still get better results? That seems like a useful way to understand whether the scaffolding is providing a lasting capability or compensating for a limitation of the current model.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute agent-system work to researchers’ limited access to large-model training resources.

r002.rationale: It predicts that stronger models may handle work now requiring designed workflows and suggests testing whether the system can be simplified as models improve.

r003.rationale: It describes some system decisions potentially being handled by the model, but does not recommend letting models make more of those decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the role of scaffolding will change as models become more capable. Right now, we often build a lot of structure around a model: we break the task into steps, manage its memory, tell it when to use tools, and add checks when it makes mistakes. Some of that structure is compensating for things the model cannot do reliably yet.

As the models improve, I would expect some of those capabilities to move into the model itself. A complicated workflow that helps today might become unnecessary, or even constrain a stronger model. So I would be cautious about assuming that every piece of scaffolding we build will remain useful across model generations.

But there is still a role for the surrounding system. The model needs access to tools, information, and feedback from the environment. You also need a way to specify what it is allowed to do. The interesting question is which parts should be learned by the model and which parts should be explicit in the system. I think that boundary will keep moving, and we should keep testing it rather than treating the current architecture as fixed.

r001.rationale: The response says scaffolding compensates for what models cannot yet do reliably, but does not attribute agent-system work to researchers’ limited access to model-training resources.

r002.rationale: It predicts that as models improve, some currently useful structure may become unnecessary, conveying that stronger models will need less scaffolding for comparable performance.

r003.rationale: It discusses which capabilities might move into the model, but does not clearly recommend that models take on more system decisions themselves.
